title: Jazz pedagogy and homogeneous teaching
summary: He says sound should be first in jazz education, criticizes homogenous academic teaching and argues for working musicians as teachers.

story.theme_name: Teaching jazz: schools, students and advice to the young
story.community_name: Becoming a teacher: jazz in schools and conservatories

blocks.x: How does jazz pedagogy help or hinder that process?

Well you know I think that there is not as much emphasis placed on that because I think musicians are more concerned with learning harmony and how to play changes and learning tunes, and you know, that’s a tricky question. But it should be all part of the © Hamilton College Jazz Archive -3-
same thing. I mean your sound, and developing a sound, is — that should be number one in jazz pedagogy, as far as I’m concerned.

Partly the reason I asked that question is because a lot of the — a number of the really veteran guys whom I’ve spoken to — sort of bemoaned the fact that the younger players, as they describe them, all sound the same. That they have learned the scales and the patterns and that you can’t recognize who they are.

There’s a very homogenous way of teaching music in jazz education, in a lot of instances. That’s why I think it’s really important to get musicians like the older musicians involved in jazz education, because their — the things that are important to them are different than maybe the typical jazz education route of someone who goes to school, gets a bachelor’s, gets a master’s, gets a Ph.D. and goes right to teaching, without having had the benefit of even spending a lot of time on the bandstand. Because you know jazz is really an experiential music and you have to play with people who are better than you. You have to get your butt kicked on the bandstand. That’s an important part of growth as a musician. But you know jazz education has kind of done a little flip flop where you know people like Yusef Lateef and Max Roach, they were hired at U Mass, I don’t know if you — I don’t think Max Roach has a Ph.D. in jazz education, but you know these days it’s almost like you have to get an advanced degree to even be considered for a jazz teaching position. And I think that’s been a change in the last couple of years, that’s kind of been the direction that it’s been going in. And I think there has to be some kind of a balance between that and getting people who are actually on the scene and touring and playing and, you know, getting them involved as well.
